title: Using WiFi You Do Not Own
drDigitalIntro:
Free WiFi in a café, hotel, or airport is genuinely useful — and it is somebody else's network.

- A café network usually opens a sign-in page before it lets you online. That page is called a captive portal.
- Giving it your email is normal. Giving it a password you use anywhere else is not — no legitimate network needs one.
- On a network you do not control, assume someone could be watching which sites you visit.
- Turn off cross-site tracking before you browse, and save banking and shopping for a network you trust.
- If a page asks you to install something to get online, close it. That is never a real requirement.

playgroundTask.scenario: Joining a café network through its sign-in page, then locking privacy down before browsing
playgroundTask.goal: You joined a public network safely and tightened your privacy

steps.say: The browser has no connection. Open the WiFi list from the bar at the top.
The café wants your email before it lets you online. That is normal — click Continue.
You are online, but on somebody else's network. Open Settings from the dock.

drDigitalSuccess: That is the whole routine for public WiFi: join through the sign-in page, hand over an email and nothing more, then turn tracking off before you browse. Do it every time and free WiFi stops being a risk.
drDigitalHint: The WiFi icon sits in the bar along the top of the screen. Once you are online, the Settings icon is in the dock at the bottom.
warning: A real café page must never ask for a password you use elsewhere. If one does, close it and stay off that network.
